title: The Winter That Destroyed Napoleon's Grande Armée
creator: Callum Pryce
description:
How the Russian winter, and one month of waiting in a burned city, destroyed the largest army Europe had ever seen.

This episode is sponsored by Winterlight Relief. Give a child a winter thermal kit: https://winterlight.org/history

Sources:
Adam Zamoyski, 1812: Napoleon's Fatal March on Moscow
Dominic Lieven, Russia Against Napoleon
Philippe-Paul de Ségur, History of the Expedition to Russia

sentences.t: By the time the Grande Armée reached Moscow in September of 1812, it had already lost something like a third of its men.
And not mostly to battle.
To disease, to heat, to desertion, to the sheer distance.
Napoleon expected the Russians to negotiate the moment he took the city.
Instead, he rode in and found it almost empty.
And within a day, Moscow was on fire.
Historians still argue about who set those fires, but the result was the same either way.
No shelter, very little food, and winter on its way.
He waited in the ruins for over a month, hoping for a letter from the Tsar that never came.
That delay is the single decision most historians point to.
Because when the retreat finally began in late October, the first snow was only days away.
I'll get into what happened at the Berezina in a second, because it's genuinely one of the most horrifying episodes of the whole war.
But first, this episode is brought to you by Winterlight Relief.
Winterlight is a nonprofit that gets emergency heating, blankets and winter clothing to families who've been displaced by war and disaster.
And honestly, after weeks of reading about people freezing on a road in 1812, it's hard not to think about the families living through winters like that right now.
Last year Winterlight reached more than sixty thousand people in Ukraine, Syria and Afghanistan.
Forty dollars covers a thermal kit for one child for the whole season, so that's a coat, boots, a hat and a sleeping bag.

Even a few dollars a month genuinely makes a difference.
Thanks to Winterlight for supporting the channel.
Okay, the Berezina.
By late November, an army that had crossed into Russia with around four hundred thousand men was down to maybe forty thousand who could still fight.
At night the temperature was dropping below minus twenty.
Horses were dying by the thousands, which meant no cavalry, no artillery, and no way to carry the wounded.
And then they reached the Berezina River, and the bridge at Borisov had already been burned.
Napoleon's engineers, mostly Dutch pontonniers, waded into water full of ice to build two improvised bridges.
They worked in shifts, standing in the freezing river, and most of them did not survive the weeks that followed.
For three days the army crossed while the Russians attacked from both banks.
On the last morning, with thousands of stragglers still on the far side, the bridges were set on fire to stop the pursuit.
The scenes on that riverbank are described in letters and memoirs in ways I'm honestly not going to read out in full.
In French, the word Bérézina still means a total catastrophe.
That's how deep it went into the national memory.
What strikes me most, going through the sources, is how few of the men who died ever fired a shot in Russia.
The campaign wasn't lost on a battlefield.
It was lost to cold, to hunger, and to one man's refusal to admit the plan had failed.
Of the roughly half a million who went in, fewer than one in ten came back across the Niemen in December.
Next week we're looking at what happened in Paris when the news finally arrived, and how Napoleon raised a whole new army in a matter of months.
If you enjoyed this one, the full source list is in the description as always.
Thanks for watching.
